chunks: Fadalah ibn Sinan, from Isma'il ibn Abi Ziyad, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), from his father (peace be upon him), who said:

Ali (peace be upon him) said: 'He who has not given death its due status is he who counts his tomorrow among his days.' And Ali (peace be upon him) said: 'A servant does not lengthen his worldly aspiration but that he ends up doing evil deeds.' And he used to say: 'If the servant were to see his death and how quickly it is approaching him, he would have loathed [worldly] aspiration and seeking the world.'
ai.seo_question: What is the effect of remembering death on a person's worldly desires and actions?
ai.summary: This narration, transmitted through the chain of Imam al-Sadiq (AS) from his father Imam al-Baqir (AS) and ultimately to Imam Ali (AS), underscores the psychological mechanism of 'long expectation' (tul al-amal) as the root of spiritual negligence. In Shia ascetic literature, this concept is pivotal, illustrating how the illusion of a long lifespan dulls the urgency of repentance and leads to the accumulation of sins. The hadith serves as a practical guide for self-accountability (muhasaba), urging believers to visualize the swiftness of death to naturally detach from worldly pursuits.

en.shaykh-tahir-ridha-jaffer: 10.Faḍālah narrated from Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Ziyād, from Abū ʿAbdillāh (a), from his father (a) who said, “ʿAlī (a) said, ‘He who counts his morrow as part of his lifetime has not given death its due status!’ ʿAlī (a) also said, ‘A servant does not lengthen his [worldly] aspiration but that he ends up doing evil deeds [to achieve his goal].’ And he used to say, ‘If the servant were to see his death and how quickly it is approaching him, he would have loathed [worldly] aspiration and seeking the world.’”
